pistons.headline: Pistons vs. Wizards final score: Cade makes history in double OT win
pistons.body:
WASHINGTON, DC - NOVEMBER 12: Cade Cunningham #2 of the Detroit Pistons celebrates against the Washington Wizards during the first overtime at Capital One Arena on November 12, 2026 in Washington, DC. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Patrick Smith/Getty Images) | Getty Images

Cade Cunningham scored a career-high 52 points, and the Detroit Pistons needed every single one of them in a 144-140 victory in double overtime against the Washington Wizards. It was not just a career-best night for Cunningham, not just one of the top-5 scoring performances in Pistons history, it was the first game in NBA history that saw a player score 50 points, dish 11 assists, and commit zero turnovers.

Cunningham simply did it all. He scored 30 points in the fourth quarter and overtime. That includes a critical 3-pointer after the Wizards had crawled their way back into the lead in the first overtime on an Anthony Davis alley-oop dunk.

The Pistons trailed 130-127 and each team had traded misses. Cunningham calmly took the ball up the left side of the floor, took a pass from Ausar Thompson, and walked into a movement 3-pointer that hit nothing but net to tie the game. On the next possession, Cade swung the ball to Duncan Robinson for what felt like a game-sealing 3 with 9 seconds left, but a video review determined Duncan had approximately 1 milimeter of his foot on the line and changed it to a two.

The scoring barrage also included critical stretch in the fourth quarter where he scored eight points and assisted another to account for 11 of Detroit’s final 12 points of the fourth quarter. Cunningham also locked up Trae Young on defense with Detroit up 119-118 in the final 30 seconds of the fourth. He forced Young into the sideline, cut off any passing lane, deflected the ball, and forced shot clock violation.

Sadly, after Cade hit two free throws to make it a 3-point game, Young redeemed himself by hitting an off-balance three from 29 feet away to give us our two overtimes of fun.

Cunningham’s performance slightly overshadowed another notable feat — Ausar Thompson tallied his first career triple-double. He was aggressive on offense driving to the rim, and delivered crisp passes in narrow lanes to keep Detroit’s offense moving.

On a night where Cade scores 52 and Ausar gets a triple-double, how the heck was it so close to begin with? How does a game like that feature 20 lead changes and 13 ties? It was a weird game.

Alex Sarr was 12-of-14 from the floor and hit his first four threes of the night. He scored 30 points and was one of three Wizards to hit the 30-point threshold. Young scored a team-high 37 points, including a perfect 17-of-17 from the line. Anthony Davis scored 30 points and added 15 rebounds.

Honestly, Detroit’s biggest issue was the same issue they’ve had all season. Their bigs were dominated and DEtroit really misses Jalen Duren. Washington outscored Detroit in the paint and were outrebounded. The biggest issue was John Collins yet again. He was a minus-18 on the night and it felt like it was even worse.

Collins started the overtime period at center in place of Paul Reed, who was a plus-25, and promptly was the primary factor in Detroit giving up a 7-0 run to the Wizards right out of the gate. It was ugly. Come back soon, Jalen Duren.

Yeah, the Pistons might be missing Duren something fierce, but they have Cade Cunningham. And that’s enough.

Rarely have I been so interested in an immediate rematch as I am in tonight’s game, which sees the Detroit Pistons taking on the Washington Wizards for the second consecutive contest. The Pistons prevailed in Monday’s game 122-111. The game was also just dang weird. Anthony Davis played out of his mind, scoring 44 points in just 34 minutes. Rookie AJ Dybantsa also enjoyed the best game of his young pro career, scoring 21 and securing eight rebounds. Everyone else on the Wizards was pretty stinky.

Conversely, Cade Cunningham had one of the worst games of the season, and Detroit was really propelled by some excellent play from John Collins and Daniss Jenkins in a new-look starting lineup. Gone are the mismatched pair of Paul Reed and Collins sharing the floor. In is Collins as a center with room to operate and Jenkins as a secondary ball handler. It’ll be interesting to see if they build off that success or if it was temporary. If Detroit can get both Collins and Jenkins playing at a high level and a locked-in Cade, it could be a blowout. pistons.headline: Pistons vs. Wizards preview:  Round two against the Wizards
pistons.body:
The Pistons and Wizards play each other again, but it is after 3 days of rest for the Pistons and the day after a game for the Wizards because the NBA used Chat GPT to generate the schedule this year or something.  This will only be the Pistons 3rd game in the last 8 days and their 2nd game against the Wizards.

The Pistons were able to control Monday’s game from start-to-finish, but the game was a little closer than it should have been because they had no answer for Anthony Davis.  Davis finished the game with 44 points and only missed 5 shots total.

The Pistons will still be without Jalen Duren, so they once again may struggle to guard Anthony Davis.  But, as Monday proved, even if they can’t stop Davis, they can still win if they stop the rest of the team.

Game Vitals

Where:  Capital One Arena in Washington DC
When:  Thursday, November 12 at 7 pm EST
Watch:  Scripps Sports Network
Odds:  Pistons (-10.5)

Analysis

There isn’t a ton more to say about this matchup that wasn’t very evident in Monday’s game.  With Jalen Duren out, the Pistons have no solution to opposing big men with any kind of offensive skill that are over 6’10”.  It seems hyperbolic, but it really has been the case.  Paul Reed is undersized and John Collins is not a natural center.  Tolu Smith has the size to possibly keep up, but he has proven to be out of his element pretty much any time he has gotten playing time so far.

The Pistons did opt to start John Collins at center against the Wizards on Monday and it did work out offensively, as he had a season-high 24 points.  But, the aforementioned Anthony Davis was able to cruise to 44 points without much resistance.  Anthony Davis always seems to have his best games against the Pistons and I wouldn’t expect him to hit a couple threes every single night, but a lot of the offense he was able to generate was off of offensive rebound putbacks or shots over the undersized players guarding him.

Surprisingly, the Pistons were only outrebounded 46-45, but they were outrebounded 14-11 on the offensive glass.  If you watched the game, you could see the Pistons lack of size rear it’s head countless times.  It is just the current state of things and something the Pistons will have to manage as best as they can for the next two weeks while Jalen Duren is still out with his hamstring injury.

The Pistons benefitted heavily from poor games out of Alex Sarr and Kyshawn George, which George in particular has been arguably the Wizards 2nd best player this season.  Trae Young also had a poor night from beyond the arc where he shot 3-of-10.  Some of that is because of how good the Pistons perimeter defense is and if the Pistons can replicate that tonight, it doesn’t really matter if they have nobody to slow down Anthony Davis.

AJ Dybantsa was able to get going a bit on Monday as he scored 21 points on 8-of-17 shooting.  There were times where he looked overwhelmed, as he had 5 turnovers, but he showed why he was the number 1 pick and a building block for the Wizards.  The Pistons have perimeter players to slow him down, but the refs were very whistle-happy on Monday which helped Dybantsa get momentum on his drives to the basket since the Pistons were not able to be as physical.

One small point of concern has been the play of Cade Cunningham over the last few games.  He had arguably his best game of the season a little over a week ago against the Charlotte Hornets and since then has really struggled, especially from beyond the arc.  He is 1 for his last 19 from beyond the arc after being close to 40% through the first seven games of the season.

He is playing more off-ball and getting clean looks, they just aren’t falling right now.  Teams are obviously focusing their defense more on Cade, but a lot of the current issues are just due to not being able to hit his outside shots.  Hopefully that changes tonight.

Luckily, Daniss Jenkins has been able to step up the last couple nights as he had a career-high, 31 points against the Lakers on Sunday and then 22 points, 6 rebounds, and 8 assists on Monday while starting.  Given the success the Pistons had starting him along with John Collins at center, I would suspect that they roll out that starting lineup again.

There were some issues defensively, which I already touched on, but the offense was much better with Collins starting and more-importantly, it finally got John Collins going after his early-season struggles.

If the Pistons are able to replicate the game they played on Monday, they shouldn’t have a difficult time defeating the Wizards, but if they let one of the other players besides Anthony Davis get hot, the Wizards have a shot at the upset.

Lineups

Detroit Pistons (7-3):  Cade Cunningham, Daniss Jenkins, Duncan Robinson, Ausar Thompson, John Collins

Washington Wizards (4-8):  Trae Young, Kyshawn George, AJ Dybantsa, Anthony Davis, Alex Sarr

Question of the Day

Do you think there is a solution to the Pistons big-man struggles or do they just need to ride it out until Jalen Duren returns?

For those of you DBB sickos who care, I’m officially a married man! We had a spooky wedding on Halloween night and spent the past week in Cabo San Lucas for our honeymoon. We had a great time celebrating over the past week and a half!

Now we’re back to Pistons hoops.

JB Bickerstaff decided to mix up the starting lineup by starting John Collins at center. Paul Reed moved to the bench, and Daniss Jenkins was inserted into the starting lineup. Detroit started small with Duncan Robinson at the 3 and Ausar Thompson at the 4.

It proved to be the right idea early, as Collins was the leading scorer for Detroit after the first quarter with nine points. The Wizards took a 32-31 lead heading into the second, behind 12 points from Trae Young and 11 from Anthony Davis.

Detroit struggled to have an answer defensively for AD, and this was another game where Detroit missed Jalen Duren’s physicality and inside presence. Davis had 30 points and eight rebounds at the halfway point while only missing one of his 11 attempts. The Pistons put up 37 points in the quarter with five different players scoring more than seven points. Collins led the way with 15, Duncan had 14, and Cade had 11 as Detroit held a 68-58 lead.

The third quarter was all about Daniss Jenkins. Cade picked up his fifth foul halfway through the third, and DJ took the reins. He made Trae Young look like a traffic cone on defense as Jenkins went on to score 13 in the quarter. He consistently attacked Young, and Young never stood a chance. Detroit continued to extend their lead as they were up 103-87 heading into the fourth.

The fourth quarter was highlighted by two beautiful plays by Ebuka Okorie and Ausar Thompson.

First, watch Ausar find Okorie in transition as Okorie does his best Kyrie Irving impression:

AUSAR TO EBUKA WE ARE IN HEAVEN pic.twitter.com/jggv5WFEeC
— Rip Haminkton (@RedAlternates) November 10, 2026

Second, the Human Swiss Army knife blocks the 7-footer Alex Sarr on one end, then follows that up by directing traffic and finding an open DJ with a great bounce pass for a wide-open dunk:

Just let Ausar do everything pic.twitter.com/3nlVa0IHKi
— Rip Haminkton (@RedAlternates) November 10, 2026

The Pistons will continue to hope for a speedy recovery for Jalen Duren as they needed his inside physicality against Anthony Davis, who finished with 44 points and 13 rebounds while shooting 16-for-21 from the field. Detroit still managed to pull away with a 122-111 win behind three different players who scored 20+ points, despite none of them being Cade Cunningham.

John Collins, in his starting small-ball five role, led the way with 24 points and 10 rebounds, shooting 9-for-13 from the field. Both Daniss Jenkins and Duncan Robinson added 22 points each, and Jenkins led Detroit with eight assists. Your fun fact of the night: Robinson led the Pistons with seven free throw attempts. There has been a clear difference in his game this year as he looks to get to the line more often. Cunningham added 17 points and seven assists.

The Pistons improve to 7-3 on the season. Detroit’s home-and-home matchup with the Wizards continues as the Pistons will travel to Washington for Round 2 on Thursday night.

Go Stones.

pistons.headline: Pistons vs. Lakers: Austin Reaves pulls a Doncic to beat Detroit
pistons.body:
DETROIT, MI - NOVEMBER 8: Austin Reaves #15 of the Los Angeles Lakers drives to the basket during the game against the Detroit Pistons on November 8, 2026 at Little Caesars Arena in Detroit, Michigan. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and/or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Brian Sevald/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images

Who needs Luka Doncic when you have the US equivalent from Newark, Arkansas, Austin Reaves? The Los Angeles Lakers guard scored a game-high 43 as his MVP-level teammate rested with a back injury, propelling LA past the Detroit Pistons 121-116.

Honestly, the game had no reason to be as close as it was in the end. The Lakers led 40-14 one basket into the second quarter courtesy of insane shotmaking (hitting 72% from the floor) and an insane amount of Pistons miscues, including having more turnovers (eight) than made baskets (six).

But the Pistons, being the Pistons, weren’t about to give up. While Detroit pulled within one point early in the fourth quarter, the Lakers led wire to wire. So while it was only marginally competitive from Detroit’s point of view, it was certainly an instructive game. Here are some of the things I learned:

1. Kevin Huerter

Kevin Huerter is going to be a critical component of the Pistons’ rotation this season. In a game where Detroit’s entire backcourt didn’t really show up to play (both Cade Cunningham and Duncan Robinson were largely no-shows until some fourth-quarter scoring), Huerter was by far the biggest bright spot for the Pistons.

It also happened to be his best game in a Detroit uniform. Huerter hit four three-pointers, scored 24 points overall, and added five rebounds, five assists, five blocks(?!) and two steals. Ever since the Pistons traded for him at the deadline last season, it was clear Huerter makes winning plays, and you were hoping he’d be able to combine that with rediscovering his 3-point shooting stroke from earlier in his career. The early returns indicate the shot might be back, as well as everything that goes with it. After tonight, he’s hitting 40% from deep this season.

2. John Collins and Paul Reed

Detroit’s starting front court simply does not work, and it will never work. For as long as Jalen Duren remains sidelined or off the floor this season, this is going to be a significant issue for the Pistons. Duren is ramping back up from a hamstring injury and will be out two more weeks. Detroit has been, and will continue to be able to weather that storm. But it ain’t pretty, and any additional time off from Duren will have me significantly worried.

Most will want to pin the blame on the newcomer John Collins, and he has certainly played worse than Reed, but I think it’s the combination that brings out the worst in both players. Each is the kind of big man that relies on the gravity from teammates that allows them to use their athleticism to create the chaos that makes them effective. With both of them on the floor, it’s two bouncy balls pinging around the floor with no semblance of a plan on how to actually get the ball to the rim. The defense is also bad, and the rebounding is even worse. It’s an ugly situation, and it was exacerbated tonight by both men getting out-physicaled by the behemoth seven-footer Walker Kessler. Kessler, the Lakers’ big offseason addition, had 12 points and 16 rebounds, including seven on the offensive end. The Lakers also dominated the Pistons in the paint, 58-46.

Again, the lion’s share of the blame goes to Collins. He’s been quite bad all season, and it’s getting less clear by the day how he’s going to turn it around and be a positive force for the Pistons. I don’t think he’s ever met a 50-50 ball he couldn’t surrender to the opposition. But the pathway to him playing well lies with sharing the floor with Duren. Get well soon, JD.

3. Austin Reaves

The Pistons were correct in trying to give Austin Reaves the bag this offseason. Detroit reportedly was ready to give the wing a max contract this offseason as the second scorer and potential missing piece in a Detroit Pistons title run. Once the Lakers believed the pending RFA had a max offer on the table, they quickly moved to get an agreement to sign him on the eve of free agency so he’d never hit the market.

Reaves was insane tonight. The degree of difficulty on his shots begged belief. He was able to create space, get balanced, and score at all three levels. It was a sight to behold, and he was by far the best player on the floor for either team tonight.

4. Daniss Jenkins

Daniss has that dog in him, especially under two scenarios: 1. There is an impending buzzer. 2. He feels like his team is getting punked. Jenkins was truly the other hero of the game behind Huerter. He hit yet another buzzer-beater tonight, and he scored a career-high 31 points. When the Pistons were down huge, Jenkins got that look in his eye, as if to say, “This is not going to happen.”

From there, Jenkins started firing away from deep, and he was hitting. In the end, he canned eight three-pointers. He was also the ONLY Pistons player to go to the free-throw line more than once in the game. Really, Jenkins is like a better version of Marcus Sasser. He’s got scoring in his blood, and he’s more of an off-guard than a point guard, despite being stuck in a point guard’s body. He’s got three inches on Sasser and better floor vision, so he’s better overall and can cosplay as a point guard better than Sass, but Jenkins works best in this Pistons lineup when he’s not running the offense.

4. The refs.

The referees love the Lakers. Nothing else needs to be said.

pistons.headline: Pistons vs Lakers preview: Best Defense vs best offense
pistons.body:
Does it get any better than the No. 1 offense versus the No. 1 defense? The Detroit Pistons find themselves in that matchup as the 122-point-per-game Los Angeles Lakers visit Motown tonight.

Luka Dončić and the Lakers put up plenty of buckets, but scoring on Detroit is still an impossible task. The Pistons only surrender 101 points a game. Smothering defense every night.

Detroit’s defense has its biggest test of the season if Dončić suits up this evening. He’s questionable with lower back tightness.

It would be a shame if we’re robbed of Cade Cunningham going head-to-head with another MVP candidate. The bigger shame would be if we miss out on Dončić versus Ausar Thompson. That matchup is like Jerry Rice versus Deion Sanders with how both are operating.

GAME VITALS

Where: Little Caesars Arena, Detroit, MI

When: 6 PM EST

Watch: TV20 Detroit/DAZN-DET

Odds: Pistons (-4.5)

Analysis

Detroit hasn’t played since Wednesday’s loss to the Philadelphia 76ers. They’ve had plenty of time to rest up. They’ll need it if Dončić suits up.

Dončić is averaging 40 points. He’s shooting 42% on nearly 14 3s a game. He gets to the line more than anybody. It’s basically no stopping Dončić at the moment. This is a Wilt Chamberlain-like hot streak. Those two are the only players to average 40 nine games into the season. Whew, to say he’s balling is an understatement.

But tasks like this are why the Pistons employ Ausar Thompson. If *anybody* can slow Dončić down, it’s the best perimeter defender on the planet. Dončić usually has success against quick defenders with wiry strength, but Ausar is bigger and stronger this season. We’ll be keeping tabs on how Ausar takes Dončić’s bumps tonight. Ausar has the quick hands to disrupt things as well.

This might be a game where we see Paul Reed getting to the level and blitzing a bunch. J.B. Bickerstaff may decide to get the ball out of Dončić’s hands and force someone else to beat them. Reed is capable of coming to the level on screens and muddying things up.

I’m sure Dončić will see some Cade tonight too. Cade won’t make it easy with his sturdy frame. On the other end, the Lakers only have a few perimeter defenders to throw at Cade.

Matisse Thybulle is firmly in LA’s rotation as he’s started all 10 games. He’s still a defensive playmaking threat. Cade deals with defenders like this nightly, but Thybulle is a plus defender nonetheless. So is Ziaire Williams. The springy 25-year-old treats every possession as if he’ll never get in the game again if he doesn’t go hard.

Those two are solid defensively, and Jake LaRavia competes. Outside of that, Detroit will have plenty of favorable matchups (Walker Kessler is a great rim protector and is off to a good offensive start. He can make a difference).

Dončić displays effort and is trying to shake the terrible defender narrative on his name, but attacking him is still the best way to slow him down. Make him work and keep him involved in actions.

Austin Reaves falls into the same boat. He’s under Dončić on the Lakers’ best defenders on the team list. Anybody with that matchup should look to be aggressive.

Reaves spends most of his time covering shooting guards. Will JJ Redick make Reaves chase Duncan Robinson all night? That’s probably not ideal. Robinson runs even great defenders into the ground.

Robinson’s light-em-up stretch continues as he’s fourth in 3s made (35). Only Dončić, Nickeil Alexander-Walker, and Steph Curry have made more.

Detroit is letting it fly from deep as a team. According to Cleaning the Glass, 40 percent of their shots are coming from 3 (15th) compared to 31 percent last year (29th). Their rim rate has flipped the other way, but getting Jalen Duren back should rectify that.

The best offense versus the best defense is a mandatory viewing appointment. Can Ausar slow down the MVP-favorite? Do the Pistons show why they’re an elite defense and smother Dončić as a team? For their first game in 11 days, the Detroit Lions take their show on the road across the Atlantic for an international Week 10 showdown in Munich, Germany, facing off against the defending AFC Champion New England Patriots.

We had the pleasure of connecting with Taylor Kyles, a staff writer for Pats Pulpit, to give us some insight into this New England squad ahead of Sunday morning’s tilt. We learned about the growing concern surrounding Drake Maye’s turnover regression, how injuries have decimated New England’s offensive line, and the coverage busts plaguing an otherwise physical defense—plus how Detroit’s offensive weapons could exploit the Patriots’ secondary in Munich:

1. The Patriots have had a bit of a Jekyll and Hyde season through nine games. It looked like they were hitting their stride after beating the Bills, Raiders, and Jets, but since then, they’ve dropped two of their last three games.

As the defending AFC Champions, what’s most concerning about this uneven start to 2026? What’s there to be encouraged by in their first half of 2026?

The most discouraging thing has been their inconsistency against upper-echelon teams outside of their division. The defense looks great against mid-tier passing attacks, but some of their schematic quirks (not using as much press and man as expected for their personnel, heavy use of disguises, spinning the dial with coverages) have been exposed against the league’s best passers. Drake Maye also regressed to his turnover-prone ways last week after over a month of clean football and MVP-caliber play.

On a positive note, Maye looked good outside of his interceptions last week while fighting for his life against the Packers’ pressure packages, so cutting back on poor decisions and throws should allow him to return to his more recent form. Defensively, they have the players to perform better than what we’ve seen, but I think the coaching staff needs to do a better job putting players in better positions to succeed and potentially simplifying things so players can do what they do best.

2. Drake Maye was six voting points away from being the league’s MVP a season ago, throwing 31 touchdowns to just 8 interceptions. 2026 has seen some pretty volatile play from Maye on a week-to-week basis, leading to him already surpassing his turnover total from a year ago through nine games.

Do you see Maye regressing from a decision-making standpoint, or is his 2026 season a victim of circumstances beyond his control?

A relatively lackluster supporting cast and a banged-up offensive line have made life difficult for Maye. A.J. Brown and Romeo Doubs haven’t lived up to expectations when on the field, and blockers Mike Onwenu, Alijah Vera-Tucker, and Reggie Gilliam are all currently on injured reserve. That said, most of Maye’s turnovers resulted from avoidable mistakes, such as forced attempts and throwing the wrong kind of pass for the situation. Maye winning Offensive Player of the Month in October showed he can rise above these issues, but we have yet to see him do it for a truly extended stretch.

3. Injuries have plagued the Patriots all season long. Where do you feel the effects of injuries are hurting this team the most? Who are some players that have made the most out of their newfound opportunities?

Injuries have most profoundly impacted the offensive line. The ground game has been limited due to the loss of both starting guards, forcing the Patriots into being a fairly straightforward downhill rushing attack. Josh McDaniel has tried incorporating different looks and wrinkles, but outside zone hasn’t really been an option with so little chemistry up front. Pass protection held up surprisingly well for a bit, but schemed pressures like blitzes and stunts have become increasingly problematic over the past three weeks, resulting in far too many unblocked pressures. There is hope things will settle down if veteran Greg Van Roten returns from IR, but he’s missed significant time and is one of the oldest players on the team, so how he performs down the stretch is anyone’s guess. Matt Pryor has emerged as a relative bright spot beside Morgan Moses, who’s been dealing with a foot injury for weeks, but the big-bodied guard can be exposed if forced to quickly redirect.

4. New England’s defense is a super interesting read from a statistical perspective. They have one of the most effective pass rushes in the NFL, and their run defense is a top-10 unit at minimum, yet they’re average as a whole unit by DVOA (15th) and below average in EPA/play (23rd).

When the Patriots defense is at its best, what are they doing successfully? Where are New England’s weaknesses on this side of the ball? Are there certain positional matchups, or player archetypes they struggle in defending?

Physicality and discipline stand out most when the Patriots are playing at their best. It’s a veteran group that plays with a lot of pride and attitude, and that translates into players swarming to the football and laying the wood when given the opportunity. Unfortunately, communication lapses and issues against tempo have led to coverage busts and big plays for opposing offenses. The defense has also struggled to take the ball away this season, which has made life tougher for both sides of the ball. This week, I’m worried about their ability to defend Jahmyr Gibbs out of the backfield. New England has yet to face an opponent that truly fed a talented receiving back through the air, but I’m not sure the defense has the linebacker or safety depth to keep Gibbs quiet if Detroit presses the issue. Jameson Williams could also have himself a day if the secondary doesn’t actively disrupt his releases and route stems.

5. The Patriots opened as 2.5-point home underdogs at FanDuel Sportsbook heading into this international matchup against the Lions. What’s one thing you want to see, what’s one thing you need to see, and one thing you’re sure you’ll see happen in this matchup between the Lions and Patriots on Sunday morning our time?

I’d like to see Drake Maye play a clean game and go toe-to-toe with Jared Goff. He had the talent to do so and elevate his supporting cast, but it will ultimately come down to picking his spots and avoiding bad decisions. I need to see a more competitive effort from the defense, particularly in the red area. This feels like a bend-but-don’t-break kind of game, so holding the Lions to field goals will be crucial. Finally, I’m sure I’ll see the Lions move the ball effectively. There are simply too many weapons for the Patriots to defend consistently, particularly without Carlton Davis. Goff will take what the defense gives him and hit a handful of shots, but again, the Patriots must be competitive once the Lions reach the red area.

lions.headline: New England Patriots vs. Detroit Lions preview: 6 key stats
lions.body:
FOXBOROUGH, MA - OCTOBER 09: Detroit Lions running back Jamaal Williams (30) blocks New England Patriots safety Adrian Phillips (21) as Detroit Lions quarterback Jared Goff (16) prepares to throw a pass during a NFL game between Detroit Lions and New England Patriots on October 9, 2022, at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, MA. (Photo by M. Anthony Nesmith/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images

Holy scheiße! The Detroit Lions’ first overseas game in over a decade, dating back to the early Jim Caldwell era, is finally here, and the Motor City militia is ready to make some noise in Munich, Germany.

While it’s still one of the more compelling European games this season, the buildup is different than expected. The Lions are coming off an emotional week that ended in a low-scoring affair in Miami, while the Patriots were bombarded by Green Bay at home. New England’s season has had its ups and downs, highlighted by a road win in Buffalo, but the team hasn’t found its mojo since the Super Bowl, aside from its head coach this offseason.

Interestingly, the game pits two tough-minded, former-player, CEO-type head coaches against each other. The Lions are looking to extend their four-game winning streak, thanks in large part to their defensive improvements, with their sights set on containing reigning MVP runner-up Drake Maye. They’ll also hope for a much better offensive performance than last time they faced the Patriots, when Bailey Zappe was the quarterback on the other side of the ball, and they got skunked.

So tap the keg and crack a few eggs, as this week’s preview will examine six key stats and matchups Detroit needs to handle to keep the winning streak train on the tracks and let you enjoy your Sunday morning kickoff.

Note: Unless otherwise indicated, all statistics are sourced from NFL Pro, FTN Fantasy, Pro Football Reference, SumerSports, or Pro Football Focus.

Pop Goes The Weasel

The Patriots’ offense heads to Germany with a bit of a MASH unit, as they’ll be down to backup offensive guards Walter Rouse and Matt Pryor. Sending my best regards to those two as they face Alim McNeill and Tyleik Williams. They’ll also be without skill-position players Romeo Doubs and TreVeyon Henderson, while A.J. Brown and Rhamondre Stevenson (161 rushing yards vs. the Lions in 2021) are questionable.

Lions fans know not to take a team lightly, even one ravaged by injuries; they only need to look back at Carolina scoring 32 points against them while missing numerous key offensive pieces. Detroit’s defense will still need to shut down the areas opposing offenses plan to attack.

Following Maye’s early-season struggles, which included a 58.6 passer rating, six interceptions, and nine sacks in the first three weeks, he has leaned into fourth-year slot receiver DeMario “Pop” Douglas, despite injuries to Brown and Doubs. Since Week 5, Douglas has recorded 22 receptions for 352 receiving yards and four receiving touchdowns. His receiving yards rank 11th among all players, just two yards fewer than Amon-Ra St. Brown in that span, while his four touchdowns are tied for third. Douglas is a career 11-yards-per-reception player, but he’s averaging 16 yards per reception over that stretch. Douglas has spent a league-leading 81.3% of his snaps in the slot during that span, with the next-closest player at just 72.5%. His 11 receiving first downs from the slot also lead the league over that stretch.

Stopping Douglas will be no easy task for the Lions’ improving defense, as Detroit allows a league-worst +0.59 EPA/pass on targets to the slot. The Lions have faced 101 slot targets (2nd), allowing 8.7 yards/pass (24th), a 10.7-yard average depth of target (30th), seven passing touchdowns (t-28th), and a 60.2% passing success rate on throws to the slot. They’ve also allowed the second-fastest average time to throw on those passes at just 2.45 seconds, nullifying much of the disruption that Aidan Hutchinson, McNeill, and any blitzes can generate.

Stopping Pop Douglas will require a dedicated effort in Kelvin Sheppard’s game plan, with Roger McCreary likely seeing plenty of time trying to burst his bubble, along with help from the linebackers and safeties. Perhaps Brian Branch will see some dedicated time against the small, shifty, but explosive Douglas. If the Lions can keep Pop bottled up in Munich, they’ll go a long way toward cutting off the Patriots’ offensive tap.

The Munich Meat Grinder

The last time the Patriots and Lions faced off, early in Dan Campbell’s second season and potentially a low point of his coaching tenure in Detroit before the team grabbed the rope and started climbing, Rhamondre Stevenson was a problem, particularly running up the middle. He recorded 11 carries for 86 rushing yards (7.8 yards per carry), including a startling 7.8 yards before contact per carry. However, things might be a little different this time around. Whether it’s Stevenson or the more diminutive Corey Kiner attempting to run up the middle against the Lions’ defense, with the aforementioned McNeill and Williams, especially without beefy guards Mike Onwenu and Alijah Vera-Tucker, they might get pounded into schnitzel.

Since Week 5, the Detroit Lions’ defense has allowed a league-best 23.3% rushing success rate on runs up the middle. That also includes just three first downs and zero rushing touchdowns allowed on 30 rushing attempts up the middle. Much like airplanes in America, they’re grounding rushing attacks up the middle.

The Patriots’ offense prefers to run up the gut, with the third-most such carries (96) this season. However, they rank outside the top 10 in yards per rushing attempt (4.1) and just 19th in both EPA/rush (-0.093) and rushing success rate (39.6%). While they rely heavily on running between the tackles, they haven’t been overly successful.

If the Lions can close down the Autobahn up the middle, they’ll force Maye to take the scenic route on third down, where Detroit’s pass rush will be waiting.

The Bavarian Bootleg

Often, when the Patriots run up the middle, they operate from under center, and their 41.5% under-center rate ranks 12th in the league. However, they struggle when Maye is crouched behind second-year pivot Jared Wilson, ranking 27th in the NFL with -0.173 EPA/play from under center. It doesn’t get much better when they use play-action from under center, either.

This season, the Patriots’ under-center play-action passing metrics have been a little startling, as they’re averaging -0.359 EPA/dropback (30th), a 12.7% turnover rate (32nd), a 61.2% completion percentage (22nd), and a 43.6% pressure rate (20th) — despite allowing only one sack.

Longtime offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels hasn’t been able to help unlock Drake Maye and the under-center play-action passing attack, and that’s music to Lions fans’ ears as Detroit continues to adjust to a linebacker corps of Derrick Barnes, Malcolm Rodriguez (possibly getting more Mike linebacker reps), and Trevor Nowaske, while also acclimating Brian Branch and newly acquired Andre Cisco into the equation. One of those Lions defenders coming up with a turnover, given that Maye has been handing out footballs like beer steins at Oktoberfest with seven turnovers on just 55 under-center play-action dropbacks, would be a welcome gift for Detroit’s overseas success.

Maye-day Parade

Where the Patriots’ offense has been buttering its bread, err, putting the bratwurst in its bun, has been from shotgun, particularly with 11-personnel.

Whether it’s operating from the ‘gun and airing it out to the likes of DeMario Douglas, Efton Chism II, Mack Hollins, and Hunter Henry, or Eli Raridon, Maye has been in an aggressive zone.

From shotgun in 11-personnel, the Patriots’ passing offense has averaged +0.176 EPA/dropback (4th), a 46.7% passing success rate (8th), 8.81 yards per attempt (2nd), an 11.66-yard average depth of target (1st), and a 12.5% explosive pass rate (4th). They’ve also managed to manufacture plenty of time to throw, averaging 3.07 seconds (1st), despite Maye still facing a 49.2% pressure rate (30th) in these situations, similar to Jordan Love at times.

While the Lions’ pass defense has struggled overall against shotgun 11-personnel, allowing +0.084 EPA/dropback (25th) and an 11.6% explosive pass rate (32nd), some metrics have been surprisingly positive. As the defense continues to improve and find itself, Detroit can take confidence in having held opposing offenses to a 42.0% passing success rate (14th), while generating a 45.4% pressure rate (3rd), a 9.0% sack rate (6th), and a 2.2% interception rate (13th) against shotgun 11-personnel passing attacks.

The game could be a lot closer than the Lions would like if Maye gets comfortable spreading the ball around from shotgun with three wide receivers in the formation. But if Detroit can limit the explosive passes and force some negative plays, it might not take 99 red balloons to send the Patriots’ offense into a panic in Munich.

Deutschland’s Favorite Sun (God)

It’s pretty surreal to see Amon-Ra St. Brown in the much-deserved spotlight this week, essentially serving as the Lions’ ambassador to Germany given his heritage. While he’s been disparagingly called a “slot merchant” by lesser talking heads in the past, St. Brown is seeing a career-low slot snap rate of 45.8% this season but has still been feasting when given opportunities from the slot.

On 73 targets to the slot this season, the Patriots have allowed 55 receptions for 690 receiving yards and five touchdowns. They’ve allowed a 75.3% catch rate (30th), 9.45 yards per target (27th), +0.455 EPA/target (27th), a 57.5% passing success rate, and a 16.4% explosive pass rate (29th).

St. Brown is due for a trip to the end zone, having gone five straight games without a touchdown (the referees robbed him of one against the Vikings), and he’ll have an opportunity to shine from the slot against a Patriots defense that has had few answers for opposing slot receivers. With Marcus Jones manning the nickel spot for New England, St. Brown could carve him up in coverage like a finely crafted German wooden nutcracker. Luckily, St. Brown mentioned on Friday that he still has two days to come up with his touchdown celebration.

Achtung! It’s a Pass!

Everyone who’s made it to this portion of the article knows that Jared Goff and the Lions’ offense rip play-action passes like the best of them. And I hate to be the bearer of bad news for the Patriots, but they haven’t been able to stop early-down play-action all season. It’s also a perfect opportunity for Goff to exorcise some lingering Super Bowl demons and exact a little revenge.

The Patriots’ defense has faced 7.9 early-down play-action passes per game, the fifth-most in the league, as opposing offenses have recognized their weakness and are attacking it. On 79 early-down play-action dropbacks, the Patriots’ defense, which will be without Carlton Davis III and features a post-injury-slumping Christian Gonzalez at cornerback, has allowed 51 completions on 71 attempts (71.8% completion percentage, 28th), 10.1 yards per attempt (30th), four passing touchdowns (29th), a league-worst +0.408 EPA/dropback, a 54.9% success rate (25th), and a 16.9% explosive pass rate (29th). Any way you slice it, the Patriots’ defense has been getting diced up on play-action passes.

You can fully expect Drew Petzing to lean into early-down play-action, putting linebackers Robert Spillane and Christian Elliss, along with strong safety Craig Woodson, in a bind while helping mitigate New England’s pass rush. That should create layups for Goff over the middle to his playmakers and potentially loosen up the running lanes for Jahmyr Gibbs, keeping defenders on their heels and in a tizzy early.

lions.headline: Detroit Lions elevate LB Owen Pappoe for Week 10 vs. Patriots

GLENDALE, AZ - SEPTEMBER 25: Owen Pappoe #44 of the Arizona Cardinals celebrates during an NFL football game against the Seattle Seahawks at State Farm Stadium on September 25, 2025 in Glendale, Arizona. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images

The Detroit Lions announced they have elevated practice squad linebacker Owen Pappoe for Week 10 against the New England Patriots in Munich, Germany.

Pappoe signed to the Lions’ practice squad just 10 days ago, after Jimmy Rolder (and eventually Jack Campbell) were placed on injured reserve. A former third-round pick of the Arizona Cardinals in 2023, Pappoe has made a career out of primarily playing special teams (49 games), but does have some experience on the defensive side of the ball as well. A highly athletic linebacker with 4.39-second speed, Pappoe can contribute in all five phases of special teams and act as an emergency option at WILL linebacker.

It’s not unusual for the Lions to roster seven linebackers on game day, given how much they value special teams, and this elevation likely reflects his quick acclimation to the Lions system and ability to contribute this Sunday.

That said, with running backs Sione Vaki (ankle, questionable) and Jacob Saylors (neck, not listed with a designation) dealing with injuries, and Vaki’s increased usage on offense, the Lions could certainly use a player like Pappoe to help fill gaps on special teams.

We will have to wait until inactives are announced ahead of the game for more details. Of note, with the Lions vs. Patriots game starting at 9:30 a.m. ET, inactives will be announced at 8 a.m. ET.

lions.headline: Dan Campbell confident Lions’ Germany travel plans will have them ready vs. Patriots
lions.body:
The New England Patriots arrived in Munich, Germany on Thursday morning. The Detroit Lions arrived on Friday morning.

Travel plans for the NFL’s ever-growing international slate have been one of the more hotly debated topics, recently ignited by the Los Angeles Rams’ expedited trip to Australia earlier in the season. They arrived the day before the game and left as soon as it ended. Their opponents, the 49ers, spent an entire week in Australia before the season opener. The Rams got wiped by the 49ers, 27-7, leading many to believe travel plans were at fault for Los Angeles’ lackluster performance.

The difference between the Lions’ and Patriots’ approach to travel is obviously not as drastic. Twenty-four hours may not make that much of a difference, but there are bound to be some who believe the Lions didn’t take enough time to adjust. Lions coach Dan Campbell tried to assure media members in attendance in Munich that they will be more than ready for Sunday’s game.

“Very confident. Very confident. I know today will be the hardest day,” Campbell said.

The last 24 hours have undoubtedly been a grueling schedule for the players. Thursday in Detroit, they had a normal day of meetings, practice, and media availability. Hours later, they were on a flight to Munich, arriving around 8:30 a.m. local time (2:30 a.m. Detroit time). Using whatever energy they recaptured from sleeping on the plane, they went right into team meetings and a walkthrough practice.

“We went from the plane; we have got settled in. About an hour later we have got into meetings, and you’re doing a little bit of the head bob,” Campbell admitted.

Still, with over 48 hours to acclimate before kickoff, Campbell is certain the team will be more than ready for Sunday’s matchup with the Patriots.

“We have got up and moved around, and I know that every eight hours here, we’re going to begin to acclimate,” Campbell said. “I know by the time we hit Sunday morning into that Sunday afternoon game, we’re going to be ready to go. So, we will be primed and ready, and I feel very good about our plan.”

lions.headline: What it’s like to witness Dan Campbell win over a room of German reporters
lions.body:
Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell opened his Munich press conference—which was attended by nearly 100 media members—with an off-kilter story. When asked what German he’d learned from Amon-Ra St. Brown, he launched into a tale about wanting to spice up the term “spread your wings” with some good old-fashioned profanity. He wanted the f-word, and when he looked it up, the closest he got was “scheiße”—the word for shit. He went for it, essentially saying “spread your shit wings.”

For us who know Campbell, that kind of clunky story is part of his self-deprecating charm. It’s undeniably funny, but it didn’t really land with the German crowd. They were either unprepared for the untraditional cadence of Campbell, or something got lost in translation.

However, for the next 20 minutes, I was able to witness what is truly a joy every time I get the opportunity to do so: watching Dan Campbell win over a room. As the mostly German press got a crash course on Campbell’s folksy accent and imperfect diction, they were also treated to his charm and authenticity. My attention quickly turned from Campbell’s answers to the media members consuming his words.

The cracked smiles that eventually gave way to unstoppable laughter. The nods of shared experience. The realization by some that they better get their phones out before this incredible answer ended.

There were two answers in Friday’s press conference where Campbell shined the most and left the crowded pub-turned-media room beaming. The first was when Campbell was asked about making his pitch for an international fan to become a Lions fan. Campbell, instead, made an entire argument for the game of football.

Campbell, as he often does when he’s about to drop bars, took his time to really think it through before answering.

“I was fortunate enough to be able to play this game before I coached it. I got to play 11 seasons. I think this is my 28th year in the NFL. I think it’s 28,” Campbell said, as he ramped up the passion. “This game, this game gave me a life, okay? I was not a superstar. I was not a speed demon. I’ve got size. I played tight end, so you do a little bit of everything. But it gave me an opportunity to make a life and do something I absolutely loved with a group of guys—at any given time, 53 men that have the same goal, and you’re all going in the same direction, and the blood and the sweat and the tears that it requires on a daily basis to be great are things you never forget.”

Buckle up, he’s just getting started.

“And it builds character. It builds character in your team, it builds character in your individual, and it allows you overcome anything in life that may come your way. I tell the team all the time, one day you’re going to get hit; you’re going to get rocked with something really tough in your life. And I hate to say it, I don’t want it to happen, none of us do, but you will. And you’re going to have to be the rock, but you’re going to know how to overcome it, and you know who you can lean on, too: your brothers who have gone through everything you’ve had to go through here.”

Campbell then snapped out of his own trance, as he often does after a long, passionate answer.

“I just think it’s special that way. And it gives guys an opportunity that may not have all the bells and whistles—just because they do all the little things right and they maximize everything that they have in their ability.”

Now drive it home with some humbleness.

“That’s the best way I could do it or say it.”

The NFL may as well cut that answer together right now, and play it at every event in which they’re trying to grow the game. But Campbell wasn’t done.

Then he cut a promo specifically about the city of Detroit and how it has shaped his football team.

“We don’t have the beach. We don’t have all this—now the summers are unbelievable, but things come a little bit harder out in that area,” Campbell said. “I always equate it to: it’s people that’ll do anything for you. They’d give you the shirt off their back if you needed it. And they’re all about doing the hard stuff.

“And when I came to Detroit to take over as head coach, man, I wanted to build a team that they could relate to. We want to be a team that they can look at and say, ‘I respect that. I respect the way they go about their business.’ That there is something gritty about it. It is hard work. It is inspiring football. It’s not the easy way out.’

“And so those are really the type of fans we have, man. Just good, wholesome people that really care about each other. They put in good days’ work and man, they back us up and support the heck out of us, and we love them to death.”

Throw some dramatic music behind that, play it before kickoff at Ford Field, and welcome the thousands of German fans who are now ready to ride with Detroit.

Campbell’s German may not go beyond “guten tag” and “scheiße,” but there is something he shares in common with the country’s culture. And he was sure to mention it in his perfect press conference dismount.

“You don’t come to Germany without getting a German beer. I know that. So, I will definitely have a beer before I leave, that’s for sure. I don’t know which one or what, but I’m getting one.”

After the dust has settled, a German reporter gleefully turned to the local Detroit beat writers and asked a question we’re accustomed to answering in the States.

“Is he always like that?”

Yes. Yes, he is.

lions.headline: Lions vs. Patriots: 3 key matchups for Week 10
lions.body:
Detroit Lions quarterback Jared Goff is hit by Miami Dolphins edge rusher Chop Robinson (44) during the first half at Hard Rock Stadium in Miami Gardens on Sunday, Nov. 8, 2026. Right tackle Blake Miller blocks. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

It’s Germany week as the Detroit Lions (6-2) travel abroad to take on the New England Patriots (5-4). Buckle up. It is about to be a wild 11-day gauntlet as the Lions play the Patriots, Tampa Bay Buccaneers, and the Chicago Bears in that span.

Meanwhile, the NFC North is absolutely insane. I love it.

This is how it was always meant to be. This is adversity.

Turn on local Detroit radio, and you’ll likely hear voices of doubt and concern. Switch to national outlets, and you’ll hear the Bears declared the favorites in the NFC, Jordan Love MVP discourse, and Kirk Cousins transforming the Vikings’ outlook as contenders.

I love it. This is how it was always meant to be.

With a win on Sunday, the Lions will take over the top spot in the NFC North with the Chicago Bears on their bye. In that event, the Lions will be 7-2 and 2-0 in the division, whereas the Bears will also be 7-2, but 0-2 in the division. All signs point to an absolute battle on Thanksgiving, as Ford Field will undoubtedly, again, welcome Ben Johnson with echoing boos.

But first, taking care of business against the Patriots and Buccaneers is priority one.

Three key matchups. Three opportunities to control the division.

Blake Miller vs. Gabe Jacas

The first key matchup is rookie versus rookie. New England’s second-round pick, EDGE rusher Gabe Jacas, Illinois, has been a disruptive playmaker from the start. For Grit Index followers, his name is not new. Jacas was one of the guys we were pounding the table for here, leading all EDGE rushers with a 9.14 Grit Index score. The Lions went with Derrick Moore, to my surprise. But an uncertain knee injury for Jacas became known after the draft process that may have been one of the contributing factors for the Lions to favor Moore.

Jacas’ early play has been impressive both as a pass rusher as well as a run defender.

#Patriots rookie EDGE Gabe Jacas continues to flash on tape. His sudden movements to shed run blocks like he does in the first clip with a swim move are impressive.

Also showed good burst to close the pocket as a looper on a stunt for a sack. pic.twitter.com/kagHHFv8fg
— Evan Lazar (@ezlazar) November 2, 2026

He plays violently with a relentless motor.

The Gabe Jacas film is so good, guys. #Patriots rookie winning with power, quickness, bend around the arc and play recognition. High level stuff. pic.twitter.com/s9i2ZJab3d
— Evan Lazar (@ezlazar) October 23, 2026

On the other side, however, the Lions have had a strong start from right tackle Blake Miller, who has had more ups than downs in his rookie campaign. Last week, however, was notably more down than his average performance.

Blake Miller is having a hard time with the Dolphins edge speed on pass rushes
— Erik Schlitt (@erikschlitt) November 8, 2026

When Jacas is lines up over Miller, my eyes will be on how the Lions’ rookie tackle responds. It will be an entertaining matchup, for sure, but also the winner of it will have a say in which team has a better flight back across the Atlantic.

Christian Mahogany vs. Christian Mahogany

The next matchup is all between the ears for left guard Christian Mahogany. After a benching for breaking team rules last week, Mahogany is back in the starting lineup. It became apparent watching the game against the Miami Dolphins that the Lions’ best five along the offensive line includes Mahogany, as Miles Frazier’s struggles impacted the Lions’ typically potent offense.

“Look, if you say you’re gonna do something, you better hold up to it, otherwise you’re gonna lose respect of the people around you,” said Dan Campbell on 97.1 The Ticket. “Because if I’m sitting in that seat and I say one thing and then I don’t do it, I would immediately lose respect for that person. So we stick by what we say we’re gonna do here.”

It is time for Mahogany to take the next step as a professional. He knows it.

Lions guard Christian Mahogany did not shed light on what team rules he broke, but talked about being benched last Sunday.

"I have to grow up," he said. "I let my teammates down, I let my organization down, and it won't ever happen again." pic.twitter.com/hx7ZhCRkMZ
— Brad Galli (@BradGalli) November 11, 2026

The time is now. If not now, Dan Campbell surely will not let one player hold the rest of the team back.

Patriots’ rookie cornerbacks vs. Lions receiving corps

With veteran cornerback Carlton Davis III already ruled out for the game, the Patriots will be leaning on two rookies to play the role opposite Christian Gonzalez. The two rookies are fifth-round pick Karon Prunty, Wake Forest, and undrafted free agent Channing Canada, TCU.

Following up on an abysmal performance against the Green Bay Packers’ paper tiger deep passing attack, the New England secondary will face an even more difficult matchup against the Lions. Following Jared Goff’s first game of the season without a passing touchdown and back-to-back games with an interception, ending his early-season streaks, Goff will be looking to right the ship against the Patriots. If I were a betting man, an Amon-Ra St. Brown anytime touchdown in his home country of Germany may be the safest bet of the weekend.

Three key matchups. Three opportunities.

Zach Libby/Maize n Brew

It’s just about that time of year. No, I’m not taking about the holiday season or when my seasonal depression kicks in — I’m talking about #FlipSZN on the recruiting trail.

Unfortunately, today’s update doesn’t favor the Wolverines, as 2027 four-star defensive back Tavares Harrington has flipped his commitment from Michigan to Ole Miss. I can only imagine he saw the Wolverines’ defense give up nearly 300 passing yards to Oregon quarterback Dylan Raiola and said, “Yeah, I’m good, fam.”

BREAKING: Four-Star Safety Tavares Harrington has Flipped his Commitment from Michigan to Ole Miss, he tells me for @Rivals

The 6’3 185 S had been Committed to the Wolverines since May

“Shark business🦈🏡”https://t.co/C2BqkK3Z9D pic.twitter.com/KQMM6ZJTmj
— Hayes Fawcett (@Hayesfawcett3) November 14, 2026

The 6-foot-3, 180-pound Chicago, Illinois native committed to Michigan back in May, following a visit for Michigan’s spring game. However, he took a visit to Ole Miss — one of the original runner-ups in his recruitment — the weekend of Nov. 7.

Harrington was one of the early building blocks of Michigan’s 2027 class. He is ranked No. 151 overall, No. 9 at the safety position and No. 8 in Illinois on the Rivals Industry Rankings. He is a versatile prospect who was recruited to Michigan as a nickel/safety.

The timing of all this is not great for Michigan, with the early signing period getting underway very soon. The program is kind of in disarray right now, too, as the Wolverines are coming off a 15-6 loss to Michigan State, offensive coordinator Jason Beck was fired, the team is (as of this writing) getting its ass kicked by Oregon, and there is plenty of uncertainty about the direction of the program. Harrington’s decision comes during a stretch when commits across the country are re-evaluating their options, and Michigan’s current struggles on the field make it harder to hang on to every pledge.

Harrington’s departure leaves a hole in a secondary class that had been one of the strongest parts of Michigan’s 2027 haul. The Wolverines still hold commitments from four-star cornerbacks Blake Jenkins and Darius Johnson, as well as three-star legacy safety prospect Charles Woodson Jr. But losing a four-star recruit that the coaching staff prioritized from the very beginning of their time in Ann Arbor takes the class down a notch.

There is also a Mount Carmel angle to monitor. Harrington comes from the same Chicago program as 2027 four-star wide receiver Quentin Burrell, who is still committed to Michigan. Will this affect what Burrell does during the early signing period? Considering Burrell committed before Harrington, it likely won’t have a major impact, but only time will tell.

The bigger concern is whether this is the start of a trend. The early signing period opens Dec. 2, and Michigan has an offensive coordinator vacancy, an uncertain head coaching situation to some outside observers, and a lot of recruiting momentum to protect. Whittingham called every single 2027 commit the night after the MSU game, and Harrington’s flip shows how hard it is to keep a class together when a season like this happens. Four-star quarterback Kamden Lopati was also at Utah last weekend, a visit that has raised some eyebrows.

For now, Ole Miss gets a win on the trail, and the Wolverines will look to fill the void left by Harrington prior to the early signing period.

michigan.headline: Game Thread: Michigan Football at No. 16 Oregon
michigan.body:
Michigan Football returns to action Saturday afternoon with another difficult road test, traveling to Eugene to take on No. 16 Oregon at Autzen Stadium.

The Wolverines (5-4, 2-4 Big Ten) are coming off arguably their most frustrating performance of the season, a 15-6 loss to Michigan State that saw the offense commit four turnovers, surrender five sacks and struggle to move the football for much of the afternoon. The loss ultimately cost offensive coordinator Jason Beck his job, with Kyle Whittingham turning to Jim Harding to take over on an interim basis.

Oregon (6-3, 4-2 Big Ten), meanwhile, enters the contest riding a two-game winning streak and coming off its biggest victory of the season, a 41-28 upset of Ohio State in Columbus. Quarterback Dylan Raiola has helped turn things around for the Ducks, throwing for 593 yards and five touchdowns without an interception over the last two games. Oregon has also climbed back into the College Football Playoff conversation, checking in at No. 16 in the latest CFP rankings.

If Michigan hopes to pull off the upset, it’ll likely need another strong showing from a defense that ranks fourth nationally in total yards allowed per game. The Wolverines are surrendering just 16.2 points per contest, but their offensive struggles have made those performances difficult to capitalize on.

Saturday also marks Michigan’s first trip to Autzen Stadium since 2003. The all-time series is tied at three wins apiece, although Oregon has won the last three meetings, including a 38-17 victory in Ann Arbor in 2024.

With just three games remaining in the regular season, Michigan still needs one more victory to secure bowl eligibility. That won’t come easily against an Oregon team with plenty left to play for.

Game Info

Matchup: Michigan Wolverines (5-4) at No. 16 Oregon Ducks (6-3)

Date: Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026

Kickoff: 3:30 p.m. ET

Location: Autzen Stadium — Eugene, Oregon

TV: FS1

Spread: Oregon -10.5

Today’s question: What do you expect from Michigan’s offense under Jim Harding?

With Beck out and Harding taking over as interim offensive coordinator, Michigan will have a new voice leading the offense against Oregon. Harding has plenty of coaching experience, but little documented experience calling plays at the collegiate level. Will the Wolverines look noticeably different offensively, or will it be more of the same? What changes are you hoping to see in Harding’s debut?

michigan.headline: Michigan Football’s young edge rushers are a bright spot in a down season
michigan.body:
Sep 19, 2026; Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA; Michigan Wolverines defensive end Carter Meadows (14) and defensive end Tariq Boney (41) celebrate a sack of Texas El Paso Miners quarterback EJ Colson (not shown) during the third quarter at Michigan Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Rick Osentoski-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

To put it bluntly, there hasn’t been much to get excited about for the Michigan football team this season. What looked like a rebound from the past two years has somehow been a bounce back into the other net — that of team “get me the hell off this train.”

The Wolverines lost to Michigan State for the first time since 2021 and their playoff hopes lie dead in the water. But if there’s any silver lining, it’s in the burgeoning, promising development of Michigan’s young pass rushers, who have slowly but surely been progressing.

Freshman Tariq Boney has steadily seen his playing time ramp up over the course of the season, as has sophomore Benny Patterson III. Meanwhile, another freshman in Carter Meadows — a former five-star recruit — has taken the longest time to make an impact on the field, but more playing time could be headed his way.

“Carter’s improving every single day,” defensive ends coach Lewis Powell told the media on Wednesday. “He’s getting bigger and stronger. He’s like a baby giraffe out there, but we love what he brings and he’ll continue to get reps as we move on here in the next three games.”

The “baby giraffe” comparison is fitting considering Meadows’ lanky 6-foot-7 build — but he also combines it with a weight of 252 pounds, meaning he’s an all-around physical specimen. He wasn’t expected to play a ton of snaps in 2026 given the guys ahead of him, but he made his debut against UTEP in September and has played snaps in each of the last four games.

But Meadows isn’t the only young lineman Powell’s thrilled about. He also had plenty to say about Boney and Patterson as well.

“Man, those guys are violent and they’re hungry,” Powell said. “And while John Henry (Daley) and Dom (Nichols) was down, these guys came, stepped up and felt like there was no difference, right? They’re both productive and we also have a new guard, and the new guard’s making strides too towards the end of the season, and we’re excited about the whole group.”

Boney’s already been able to turn his snaps and physical tools into production, logging 10 total tackles, three tackles for loss and two sacks. And Patterson — the oldest of the trio — has also flashed, playing in every game since Week 2 and logging 22 total tackles and four tackles for loss.

Benny Patterson made quite a few plays Saturday.

He blasts the OT, and the Guard can’t do anything with him.
5 yard TFL for Benny. pic.twitter.com/lfnSZ6iGTo
— Due# (@JDue51) November 3, 2026

The Wolverines were always expected to play a deep rotation at edge. But injuries to Daley and Nichols, the prospective leaders of this pass rush, have opened up a path for the young group. And that group has already shown they can step up and take on an increased burden.

With Nichols and Daley both set to leave the program in the next couple years, it’s very likely that Patterson, Boney and Meadows will be involved in the transition from the old guard to the new.

michigan.headline: 3 Keys to Victory: Michigan Football at Oregon
michigan.body:
ANN ARBOR, MI - NOVEMBER 2: The Oregon Duck mascot signals no catch during a game between University of Oregon and University of Michigan at Michigan Stadium on November 2, 2024 in Ann Arbor, Michigan. (Photo by Michael Miller/ISI Photos/Getty Images) | Getty Images

The two programs meeting in Eugene this weekend could not be going in any more opposite directions. Michigan is now 5-4 losing to Michigan State for the first time since 2021, and Oregon is coming off a huge win over Ohio State in Columbus.

If head coach Kyle Whittingham wants any chance at survival, he’s going to need this one. Here are three keys to Michigan pulling off the upset.

Run the ball

It’s still quite shocking just how bad Michigan’s run game has been this season. The Wolverines rank 109th in FBS in rushing yards per game with 128.7. The last time Michigan finished with a rushing yards per game lower than that was in 2013 when it ran for 125.7 yards per game.

Oregon is a team that lives and dies by its run defense. The Ducks rank 40th in FBS by allowing 124.8 rush yards per game. But in all three of their losses, the Ducks have allowed 140 or more rushing yards. In all six wins, they’ve allowed less than that mark.

Whether it be any of the three running back options — Jordan Marshall, Savion Hiter or Bryson Kuzdzal — it doesn’t really matter as long as the run game gets established. The hope is having offensive line coach Jim Harding calling plays will put more of an emphasis on run blocking and downhill running. But based on recent history with this offense and how the offensive line has performed, it seems like a long shot.

Win the turnover battle

Last Saturday’s game was the latest example of how the turnover margin has killed Michigan all season. Going into the game, the Wolverines had a -4 turnover margin on the year — they proceeded to double that against the Spartans with four turnovers and no takeaways on defense.

The best game of the season in terms of turnover margin was also arguably its best win over Oklahoma where it had a fumble recovery and interception, ending with a +2 turnover margin. The only other game with a positive turnover margin was against Penn State.

Oregon, on the other hand, has an even turnover margin. The Ducks sit pretty squarely at a +1, 0 or -1 margin each game, but the two outliers were -4 in the loss to UCLA and +4 against Portland State in an 84-0 victory. Needless to say, if the Wolverines are to have any chance at winning, their defense is going to need to help out the offense even more than it already does by generating more turnovers.

Start fast to quiet Autzen Stadium

Michigan is going to also need help in as many of the intangibles as possible. Autzen Stadium is often credited as one of the loudest stadiums in college football. Even though they’re only 5-4, the Ducks are coming off a huge win and hosting a program like Michigan is sure to get the crowd fired up — not to mention the comments between Whittingham and Oregon head coach Dan Lanning this week.

In quarterback Tommy Carr’s first two wins — Penn State and Rutgers — he and the offense scored a touchdown on their first drive from scrimmage together, the first of the second half vs the Nittany Lions and first of the game vs the Scarlet Knights. The Wolverines getting help in that department by scoring early could bring a lot of confidence to a group that was decimated last week against a mediocre Michigan State defense.

All the midseason change — from quarterback to offensive coordinator — hasn’t left much continuity for the Wolverines to establish any semblance of a rhythm. But going into Autzen and scoring on the first drive would help the offense’s momentum and help the defense responds.

msu.headline: Getting To Know The Enemy: 6Qs About The Washington Huskies
msu.body:
SEATTLE, WA - OCTOBER 09: Washington head coach Jedd Fisch instructs the official during the college football game between the Washington Huskies and the Iowa Hawkeyes on October 9, 2026, at Husky Stadium in Seattle, WA. (Photo by Jesse Beals/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images

Happy Thursday, TOC Nation. Our Michigan State Spartans Football Team is riding high after knocking off um, and is now looking to turn that into some momentum for the final quarter of the season. I sat down with Mark Schafer from UW Dawg Pound to learn about this weekend’s foe, the Washington Huskies. Let’s see what he had to say.

The Only Colors: This is year 3 for Washington in the Big Ten. How are you enjoying life in your new conference? Do you feel like the distance component of many of your games is an issue?
What were your expectations coming into 2026?

Mark Schafer:  While I do like the variety in all of the teams the Huskies face, and I do think it’s interesting to
see how the Huskies slot into the pecking order of the new Big Ten, part of me misses the old regional based conferences. But, right, wrong or otherwise, this is the business we’ve chosen. So I like it from a competition standpoint, but I do miss being in the PAC 12 sometimes. Part of that is the distance component. Before this year, Jedd Fisch’s major pitfall as a coach was his inability to win outside of the Pacific Time Zone. He has surprised some by winning both conference road games outside of the Pacific Time Zone (at Purdue and at Nebraska). However, the team has fallen well short of expectations for this season. Ranked at 17 to start the year, there was talk of a playoff berth with all the talent on offense and defense. However, that talent has yet to translate into many decisive victories, which has been incredibly maddening. In my mind, it comes down to 2 men, the head coach and the starting quarterback.

TOC: Your quarterback is Demond Williams Jr. He got knocked out of the sixth game of the season with an injury, missed a game, got put in late in the following game, and then started your most recent game – a loss to Penn State. Washington did win the 2 games he did not start, though Williams was on the field for the Huskies’ only offensive TD of the latter one. Is he the better QB option? What are his strengths and weaknesses?

MS: For starters, because of his athletic ability, I believe that he is a better option over Elijah Brown (who gets the ball out faster but doesn’t have the best arm). But don’t mistake this for him being head and shoulders above the competition. He has regressed in terms of his decision making from a pretty good 2025 season. It seems like he holds onto the ball too long and doesn’t know what to do when you pressure him, which results in him sailing throws, overshooting on deep shots, and missing receivers when he should be hitting them in stride. It also seems like he’s trying too hard to make a big play and he forces it when it’s not there. But it’s also part of the Demond Williams experience, because when he does make the big play, it gives the Huskies the shot of momentum they often need to sustain drives. Most of the time, it’s frustrating, but when he gets going and takes what’s there, he can be a pretty good quarterback. The issue is the consistency is not where it should be in year 3.

TOC: Who are the skill position players on Washington that MSU fans should worry about?

MS: The wide receivers are particular standouts. Due to the rash of injuries to the running backs, both
Chris Lawson (the Huskies’ leading receiver with 48 catches, 727 yards and 3 touchdowns) and
Dezmen Roebuck (who leads the team in receiving touchdowns with 4) have seen occasional
time in the backfield. They are great receivers with incredible athletic ability, and Lawson
especially has been a particularly surprising breakout. At tight end, the 270 pound Baron Naone
serves as Demond Williams’ primary safety valve. With 21 catches, 275 yards receiving and 3
touchdowns, the big guy has shown supreme athletic ability for his size, and emerged as an
unexpected TE1 (a role Husky fans expected would go to Decker Degraaf).

In the backfield, it’s been a struggle, as the committee of Trey Cooley (a 6th year senior) and Brian Bonner (a true
Freshman 4 star) have shouldered the load to frustrating results, though Bonner has shown
flashes that suggest he could be a star. I blame that on injuries, as season opening RB1 Quaid
Carr and Jayden Limar have been sidelined for much of the season, but Limar came back for the
Nebraska game and had a team high 66 yards against Penn State. But thanks to said injuries, this
team is pass first, second, and third.

TOC: What is the base formation of the Huskies’ defense? Which level of the defense is its best? Who is the one name on this side of the ball that the MSU coaching staff must scheme for?

MS: DC Ryan Walters runs a base 4-2-5 defense, but uses a lot of exotic looks to disguise what he actually is going to try to do, often sending defenders on late blitzes for instance. In terms of personnel, I’d say that the secondary is the best unit of the defense. With talent like safety Rylon Dillard Allen (43 tackles, 2 pass breakups, 3 picks), nickel Dylan Robinson (37 tackles, 4 pass deflections, 1 interception), freshman cornerback Jeron Jones (22 tackles, 3 pass deflections, 2 interceptions), and Emmanuel Karnley (who leads the team is pass deflections with 11), that group has been by far the best on the defensive side of the ball. But the best player on defense is Alex McLaughlin. McLaughlin is a high motor guy who is in on seemingly every play, leading the team in tackles (with 63) and interception return yards (52), and who also has 3 defensive touchdowns in his 2 years at UW. It’s tough to scheme for him because he has great instincts, and hits hard lining up everywhere on the field.

TOC: Fill in the blank: Washington will win if ___. Washington will lose if ___.

MS: UW will win if they can keep Demond Williams comfortable and allow him to get the ball to his
receivers in space where they can make plays (which in my opinion is where he excels the most).
It also won’t hurt to get the running game going if they can, even if that means doing so with
screens or receivers in the backfield.  Any extra option to get yards without relying on one guy is
always good. Defensively, it really comes down to keeping everything in front of them, and
doing that early is key because I, and most other fans, do not prefer wild comebacks and swings
in momentum like last week. If the defense plays like they did in the first half last week (a
distinct possibility), and the offense continues its slide into something worse than mediocrity,
they will lose.

TOC: Predict the final score.

MS: I predict a low scoring first quarter, Michigan State to slightly pull away and for the Huskies to be down at half, before a few momentum swinging plays allow the Huskies to pull out the victory.
Washington-17, Michigan State-14

TOC: Bonus question: Aside from former athletes, who is Washington’s most famous alum?

MS: UW has plenty of non-athlete alums who are notable. Frank Herbert (author of Dune) went to UW, as did Beverly Cleary (author of the Ramona Quimby series of children’s books), smooth jazz saxophonist Kenny G, Ken Jennings (owner of a 74 day winning streak on Jeopardy!, and now the show’s host), Rainn Wilson (known for playing the role of Dwight Schrute on The Office), and the late great Bruce Lee. Joel McHale (best known for playing Jeff on Community) is a unique case, as he was actually a walk on tight end for 2 seasons, though he did not play in any games.

msu.body:

Hard to believe we are now in the last quarter of the 2026 football regular season and the Spartans have just two more games in Spartan Stadium.  The first is this Saturday against the Washington Huskies (4:15 PM ET, BTN).  Here, we’ll take a closer look at the Huskies and some of the storylines for this game.
